To find the greatest number of vertices Rose can make red, we model the board as the additive group $\mathbb{Z}_n$ with $n = 1001$. Without loss of generality, let the chip initially start at vertex $0$.

### 1. Brunno's Strategy (Upper Bound)
The prime factorization of $1001$ is:
$$1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$$
The smallest prime divisor of $1001$ is $p = 7$. Thus, the largest proper subgroup $H \subset \mathbb{Z}_{1001}$ has order:
$$|H| = \frac{1001}{7} = 143$$

The quotient group $\mathbb{Z}_{1001} / H \cong \mathbb{Z}_7$ partitions the board into $7$ cosets of size $143$. The starting position $0$ belongs to the coset $H$. Brunno can choose any other coset $W = c + H$ (where $c \not\equiv 0 \pmod 7$) and commit to never letting the chip enter $W$.

Suppose the chip is currently at some vertex $x \notin W$. For any integer $k$ chosen by Rose, the two possible destinations are $x + k$ and $x - k$. If both were in $W$, we would have:
$$x + k \equiv c \pmod H \quad \text{and} \quad x - k \equiv c \pmod H$$
Adding these congruences gives:
$$2x \equiv 2c \pmod H \implies x \equiv c \pmod H$$
(since $\gcd(2, [G:H]) = \gcd(2, 7) = 1$, division by 2 is valid). This implies $x \in W$, which contradicts $x \notin W$.

Hence, it is impossible for both destinations to lie in $W$. Brunno can always choose the direction that avoids $W$. Consequently, the chip will never visit any of the $143$ vertices in $W$, leaving them white forever. Thus, Rose can make at most:
$$1001 - 143 = 858 \text{ vertices red.}$$

---

### 2. Rose's Strategy (Lower Bound)
Suppose the game reaches a point where Rose can no longer force any new vertex to be painted red. Let $R$ denote the set of red vertices, and let $W = \mathbb{Z}_n \setminus R$ be the set of remaining white vertices. 

The chip is currently at some vertex $x_0 \in R$. Since Rose cannot force the chip to visit any new vertex, Brunno can keep the chip within $R$ indefinitely. Let $R_{\text{safe}} \subseteq R$ be the set of vertices in $R$ from which Brunno can remain in $R$ forever. Clearly, $x_0 \in R_{\text{safe}}$, so $R_{\text{safe}} \neq \emptyset$.

From every $x \in R_{\text{safe}}$ and for any $k$, at least one of $x+k$ or $x-k$ must be in $R_{\text{safe}}$. In other words, no $x \in R_{\text{safe}}$ can be the midpoint of two elements in the complement $W' = \mathbb{Z}_n \setminus R_{\text{safe}}$. Therefore, for any two elements $u, v \in W'$, their midpoint:
$$m = \frac{u+v}{2} \pmod n$$
must also belong to $W'$. 

In any finite abelian group of odd order, a non-empty subset closed under taking midpoints is necessarily a coset of a subgroup. Since $R_{\text{safe}} \neq \emptyset$, $W'$ is a proper subset of $\mathbb{Z}_{1001}$, meaning $W'$ is a coset of a proper subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{1001}$.

The largest proper subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_{1001}$ has order $143$. Since $W \subseteq W'$, we have:
$$|W| \le |W'| \le 143$$
which implies:
$$|R| = 1001 - |W| \ge 1001 - 143 = 858$$

Hence, Rose can always make at least $858$ vertices red.

ANSWER: 858
